title: How a Bengaluru Couple's Homesickness Built India's Hottest Dosa Brand
excerpt: Akhil Iyer and Shriya Narayan turned a craving for Davangere-style benne dosa into a Rs 350 crore brand with three Mumbai outlets, a Delhi presence, and billionaire investor interest.
body:
• Benne, founded by Bengaluru couple Akhil Iyer and Shriya Narayan, grew from a 275-sq-ft Bandra outlet in May 2024 to a multi-city dosa chain valued at Rs 350 crore
  • Claypond Capital, the family office of billionaire Ranjan Pai, is in early-stage talks to invest Rs 35–40 crore — its first bet in the food and beverage sector
  • The brand serves 1,000–1,200 plates daily in Mumbai alone across three locations, plus a Delhi outlet, with zero traditional marketing spend

Two years ago, Akhil Iyer and Shriya Narayan were a film producer and a psychologist with no restaurant experience and no investors — just a persistent craving for a dish they couldn't find in Mumbai. Today, their dosa chain Benne is valued at Rs 350 crore and drawing interest from one of India's most prominent family offices.

A Craving That Became a Company

Iyer had lived in Mumbai for 11 years before launching Benne. Every trip back to Bengaluru ended with a plate of Davangere-style benne dosa — thick, crisp-edged, drenched in white butter — before he could bring himself to board the return flight. "Benne" means butter in Kannada, and the dish, credited to a woman named Chennamma in 1930s Davangere, has been a staple of Karnataka's darshini culture for decades.

Narayan, a psychologist who moved to Mumbai after marrying Iyer, recognized the craving as something deeper than hunger — it was about identity and the city they'd left behind. For two and a half years, the couple talked about bringing authentic benne dosa to Mumbai. In May 2024, they opened a 275-square-foot, 12-seat outlet in Bandra, designed to feel like the no-frills darshinis they grew up eating at.

"Two people from Bengaluru, living in a city that gives you everything except the thing you miss most, decided to stop missing it and start making it."

— Christine Joseph, LinkedIn

From 12 Seats to 1,200 Plates a Day

Mumbai responded immediately. Long queues formed within weeks. Viral Instagram reels and visits from Deepika Padukone, Ranveer Singh, Virat Kohli, and Anushka Sharma turned Benne from a neighborhood find into a citywide sensation — all without a rupee spent on traditional advertising.

The brand has since expanded to three Mumbai outlets and a Delhi location in Greater Kailash II. According to The Hindu BusinessLine, Benne now serves 1,000–1,200 plates a day in Mumbai alone. Customers order through self-service kiosks and watch chefs, trained in Bengaluru, work batter on custom 300-kg cast-iron tawas through glass-panelled kitchens.

The menu stays tight: benne dosa served with a spicy tomato-onion chutney and a coconut-mint variant — no sambar, no sprawling menu, no table service. The format is built for quick turnover, and it works.

A Rs 350 Crore Valuation

According to a Moneycontrol report, Claypond Capital — the family office of billionaire investor Ranjan Pai — is in early-stage talks to invest Rs 35–40 crore in Benne at a valuation of roughly Rs 350 crore. The deal would mark Claypond's first investment in the food and beverage sector; the firm has previously backed Akasa Air and Zepto. Benne had earlier raised funding from venture firm Peercheque.

"I don't think Benne has been overvalued at 350 crore," actor and food commentator Kunal Vijaykar told Storyboard18. "If they are planning to scale, it will cost money. Plus brand value is so difficult to actually put a figure on."

Part of a Larger South Indian QSR Wave

Benne's rise comes amid a broader boom in premium South Indian quick-service chains. The Rameshwaram Cafe recently opened a 6,500-sq-ft Mumbai outlet serving nearly 20,000 dosas and idlis daily. Cafe Amudham, backed by Zerodha co-founder Nikhil Kamath, is scaling similarly. Legacy chains like Banana Leaf have added benne dosa to their menus.

The darshini format offers compelling economics: a kiosk costs Rs 20–30 lakh to set up, lean staffing delivers higher revenue per square foot, and rising LPG costs are making the tight-menu model increasingly attractive to operators and investors alike.

What's Next

"Hype takes you only so far," food writer Kalyan Karmakar told Storyboard18. "But if the product is good and consistently good, which is in the case of Benne, then it is quite possible to keep the demand sustainable." For Iyer and Narayan, the challenge is familiar to any fast-growing food brand: scale without losing what made people line up. Their answer appears to be the same discipline that shaped the original outlet — a tight menu, authentic preparation, and no shortcuts on the butter.
nri_angle: Benne dosa is a Bengaluru staple now expanding nationally, part of a broader wave of regional Indian food brands gaining mainstream attention and investor interest.
author: Diaspora Desk
